discovery: The titanium-sapphire laser and passive mode-locking (Kerr-lens and semiconductor saturable-absorber), creating the practical femtosecond laser
motivation: Modern ultrafast science rests on a laser medium and a way to mode-lock it. Peter Moulton's titanium-doped sapphire laser (1982) gave a broadband, tunable gain medium that can support femtosecond pulses. Wilson Sibbett's group discovered self-mode-locking of Ti:sapphire in 1991, explained as Kerr-lens mode-locking, which made sub-10-femtosecond pulses routine and reliable. Ursula Keller invented the semiconductor saturable absorber mirror (SESAM), which made passive mode-locking robust across solid-state lasers and spread ultrafast sources into industry and medicine. Together these advances made the femtosecond oscillator that seeds nearly every chirped-pulse amplifier, frequency comb and attosecond experiment. They also opened femtochemistry, multiphoton microscopy, strong-field physics and precision metrology. Prizes have honoured the physics these tools made possible, but the oscillators themselves have never been recognised.
